lawyer:
Asrarul Hossain with Sk. Abul Hossain and Syeda Afsar Jahan, Advocates ------- For the Petitioner. 
Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate ------- For the State.
parties:
Dhaka Dyeing & Manufacturing Company Ltd.  ------- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Chairman Second Labour Court Dhaka & others  ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury, J.: Writ Petition Nos. 298 and 299 of 1985 are taken up for disposal analogously as these arise out of the same order passed by the learned Chairman, Second Labour Court, Dhaka in Complaint Case Nos. 39 and 41 of 1983. 

 2. The facts leading to these Rules are that one Md. Abul Hashem Khan and another Md. Ibrahim filed the two aforesaid Complaint Cases before the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka alleging that they have been working under the petitioners before us as Tailors with clean records since 1969 and they also acted as office-bearers of the Trade Union of the workers at the factory of the present petitioner. Their further case is that out of grudge the present petitioner issued charge sheets and show cause notices against them on certain allegations on 9.3.83. They replied thereto on 15.3.83 but their replies were not considered and found to be unsatisfactory and the 2nd party petitioner with malafide intention violating the provisions of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 dismissed them from their services. Their further case is that the order of dismissal was passed without holding any proper enquiry and witnesses were not examined by the enquiry committee in presence of the delinquent petitioners nor their witnesses were examined. Their further case is that they submitted grievance petition on 10.5.83 and got the reply on 1.6.83 in respect of Md. Abul Hossain Khan and on 22.5.83 in respect of Md. Ibrahim. The Company by order dated 3.5.83 dismissed the respondents from service. Thereafter these dismissed employees filed the aforesaid complaint cases before the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka. 

 3. The present petitioner before us contested the aforesaid two cases by filing separate written statements denying the material allegations contending that the employees were dismissed by letter dated 3.5.83 on charge of misconduct and that was done after compliance with the requirements of law and after giving necessary opportunities to the employees for their defence. Their further case is that these employees were charge sheeted for gross misconduct, for negligence of their duties and for intentionallly damaging the cloth meant for export and causing loss to the Company as detailed in the charge-sheet dated 9.3.83. They were also asked to show cause and when they showed cause on 15.3.83 those were found to be unsatisfactory and the enquiry committee was set up to hold the enquiry. The enquiry committee held that enquiry with due notice to the employees which were attended by these delinquent employees and they were afforded opportunities to defend themselves. The enquiry committee then found them guilty and on consideration of their past record the Management dismissed the respondents from service. 

 4. Both the parties adduced evidence before the learned Labour Court who after consideration of all the materials on record by his order dated 14.7.85 allowed the cases and ordered for reinstatement of the respondents in their service within 45 days from the date of the order. The petitioners being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with this order of the learned Labour Court moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rules. 

 5. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned Labour Court failed to appreciate that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court was only to see as to whether procedural requirements of law were duly complied with by the employer in awarding punishment for misconduct of an employee and not to enter Into the merit of the allegations and it cannot act as an Appellate or Revisional authority. He further submits that the Labour Court committed an error In holding that there was nothing in evidence that the petitioner suffered any loss for negligence of duty by the respondents and that the petitioner actually exported bed covers in question. He also submits that while disposing of the cases and giving relief to the respondents the Labour Court committed illegality in assessing the evidence adduced before the domestic tribunal and he also made out a third case when he found that the respondents cured the defect by sewing again the defective bed covers and there is no evidence that the petitioner suffered any loss and that the respondents made such defects out of negligence and with a motive to cause loss. 

 7. Admittedly the respondent No. 2 of Writ Petition No. 298 of 1985 Md. Abul Hashem Khan and respondent No. 2 of Writ Petition No. 299 of 1985 Md. Ibrahim were the workers of the petitioner Company and they were dismissed from service by the Company on 3.5.83 for misconduct. It is also an admitted fact that these respondents were charge sheeted and there was an enquiry conducted by the enquiry committee constituted for the purpose and on the basis of the report of the enquiry committee these 2 respondents of the Writ petitions were dismissed from service against which they moved the learned Labour Court in 2 aforesaid Complaint cases. It appears that the learned Labour Court after examining the witnesses and on perusal of the records came to the finding that there is nothing in evidence that the 2nd party suffered any loss or the 1st parties of the 2 cases made the defects due to negligence and with motive to cause loss. The learned Labour Court found that the allegations against the respondents in the charge sheet were not established. We have carefully gone through the judgment of the learned Labour Court and it is found that the Labour Court while allowing the cases entered into the merit of the case and assessed the evidence. It is well settled in the case of the Manager Zeal Bangla Sugar Mills Ltd. reported in 34 DLR I that the Labour Court is not a Court of appeal. It can interfere only when the enquiry officer or the committee acts unfairly and against the principles of natural justice. Its function is to see whether the delinquent is lawfully punished. 

 8. It has also been held in the case of Bikash Das reported in 29 DLR (SC) 280 that when an order of a domestic tribunal is challenged all that the Court is to see, is that whether the charge framed against the delinquent was such as constituted an offence or default which calls for a penal action and that the employee was given an opportunity to defend himself in allowing him to cross-examine the witnesses and to call evidence in his support and that the tribunal was constituted by impartial persons and that there were materials before the domestic tribunal to come to a finding. 

 9. Here in the present cases before us the enquiry committee was constituted to hold an enquiry  on the charge: framed against the respondents and the  enquiry committee proceeded with the :enquiry after  giving due notices to the delinquents and they recorded the evidence in presence of these employees who refused to cross-examine some of the witnesses and cross-examined at least one and the enquiry committee after giving due and all the opportunities to the delinquents submitted the report and on the basis of that enquiry report the Company dismissed the respondents. This indicates that the enquiry committee followed the procedure laid down in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders), Act 1965 in conducting the enquiry. There is, therefore, no defect in the enquiry. The allegations that the enquiry committee proceeded with the enquiry without affording an opportunity to the delinquent employees for cross-examining the witnesses and adducing their evidence has got no leg to stand upon. It is, therefore, found that the enquiry committee followed the procedure as laid down in law. The learned Labour Court also has not found that the procedures as set forth in the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, has not been followed. It appears that the learned Labour Court on consideration of the evidence and reassessment of the same came to the finding that the charge sheets against the delinquents have not been substantiated. This means that the learned Labour Court acted as an appellate Court. It is well settled that in deciding such cases the Labour Court cannot act as an appellate Court. Agreeing with decision reported in 34 DLR 1 we are of the view that in the present cases the Labour Court acted beyond jurisdiction in re-assessing the evidence examined by the domestic enquiry committee and it acted without lawful authority in sitting as an appellate Court over the finding of the domestic enquiry committee constituted by the employer. It is also well settled in the case of S.H. Quddus and others reported in 33 DLR 1 that it is not the function of the Labour Court to make re-assessment of evidence recorded by the tribunal. The b fact that on re-assessment of the evidence by some other person a different findings could have been arrived at is not a ground to hold that the enquiry was improper or unfair. Agreeing with this decision we are of the view that the learned Labour Court in the facts and circumstance of the case acted without lawful authority. 

 11. Having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record we hold that the learned Labour Court acted without any lawful authority in allowing the complaint cases only on the grounds that the charges against the delinquents have not been established and it requires interference. 

 12. The Rules are accordingly made absolute without any order as to costs. The order dated 14.7.85 passed by the Labour Court in Complaint Case Nos. 39 and 41/1983 is found to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. Send down the original case records at once.
